title: "Slow as Molasses"? The 1919 Flood That Killed Twenty-One
parts: There's an old saying: "slow as molasses."
On January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen, a flood of molasses killed twenty-one people in Boston.
It moved at highway speed.
The cause was not sabotage, even though a company said so in court.
We will mark every claim: documented, disputed, or myth.
By the end, you will know why this "slow" liquid turned lethal that day.
You will also hear why the two best explanations — one about physics, one about engineering — are both more careful than the story usually told.
Welcome to The Everyday Mystery.
Midday, January fifteenth, nineteen nineteen. The North End of Boston.
A steel tank over fifteen meters tall, owned by the Purity Distilling Company, a subsidiary of United States Industrial Alcohol, collapsed.
It released a wave of molasses meant for making industrial alcohol — not food syrup.
Twenty-one people died. About one hundred fifty were injured.
Most deaths came from being crushed by debris, or trapped and suffocated in the molasses. Documented.
The company's first defense: anarchists blew up the tank.
They pointed to a threat received a year earlier, and a bomb found at another of their sites in nineteen sixteen.
Years of litigation followed. A court-appointed auditor rejected that theory for lack of evidence.
Myth.
In nineteen twenty-five, the auditor, Hugh Ogden, concluded the real cause was negligence: the tank was built and inspected badly.
The case produced thousands of pages of testimony before that ruling.
Documented: sabotage, rejected. Negligence, confirmed.
Decades later, a researcher named Nicole Sharp led a deeper look at the physics.
In twenty sixteen, she presented the work at a meeting of the American Physical Society.
That is a conference presentation, not a peer-reviewed paper in a journal — no later publication was found.
Her team studied historical records, old maps, weather data, and how cold molasses actually behaves.
Documented, with that limit on its status noted.
Their key finding: the molasses had arrived from the Caribbean still warm, and had not fully cooled to Boston's winter temperature.
Once it spilled, the cold outside air thickened it fast — Sharp estimated the viscosity may have risen by a factor of four or more.
That thickening likely made it harder to rescue people trapped inside it.
In warmer weather, the same spill probably would have cost few or no lives. Documented, as the study's own reading.
You may have heard the wave hit thirty-five miles an hour, nine meters high.
That number comes from accounts written in nineteen nineteen — not a fresh measurement by the twenty-sixteen team.
Disputed: historical estimate, not a new calculation.
There is a second explanation, from engineering, not physics.
Ronald Mayville, a structural engineer, spent years studying the tank's failure.
His finding: the steel walls were far thinner than they should have been, and the steel itself was low in manganese — brittle in cold weather.
His modeling points to a crack starting at a rivet, right above an inspection hatch that was barely reinforced.
Documented, as his conclusion.
Mayville himself is careful here.
Even after more than twenty thousand pages of conflicting testimony in the original case, he says the exact cause was never determined for certain.
His work is the most cited modern explanation — not the final word.
Let's count what we actually know.
A tank collapsed in Boston in nineteen nineteen, killing twenty-one people: documented.
Anarchists blew it up: myth.
Exactly why the structure failed, down to the last detail: still disputed by the field's own experts.
So why did something "slow as molasses" move fast enough to kill?
Cold turned it into something closer to a solid wave, and a cheaply built tank gave way first.
The company was found negligent, not murderous — and more than a century later, engineers are still arguing over exactly where that first crack began.
